Abstract The Doyle–Kirmse reaction represents a powerful synthetic
tool for forming both C–S and C–C bonds in a single process. The rhodi-
um-catalyzed Doyle–Ki rmse reaction of S-allyl and S-propargyl phos-
phorothioates with diazoesters has been developed and represents a
rare example involving substrates  bearing an elec tron-withdrawing
group on the sulfur atom. The transformation takes place at room tem-
perature, in only 5 minutes, and leads via a [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrange-
ment of the sulfonium ylide intermediate to the corresponding S-ho-
moallyl or S-homoallenyl phosphorothioates in yields ranging from 25%
to 92% (19 examples).
Key words Doyle–Kirmse reaction, [2,3]-rearrangement, propargyl
sulfides, allyl sulfides, diazoesters, phosphorothioates, C–S bond forma-
tion
The Doyle–Kirmse reaction is a powerful method for
forming both C–S and C–C bond s in a single process, en-
abling the synthesis of a wide  range of homoallyl or ho-
moallenyl sulfides.1 The metal-catalyzed version consists of
the reaction of an allyl or a propargyl sulfide and a metal
carbene species classically generated by the decomposition
of a diazo compound (Scheme 1, A). This leads to the key in-
termediate of this reaction which is a sulfonium ylide that
can be either metal-bound or metal-free depending mainly
on the nature of the substrate and metal. The resulting ylide
can then evolve through a [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement
to the corresponding homoallyl or homoallenyl sulfide. Var-
ious transition-metal complexes, mainly based on rhodium
and copper, but also on ruthenium, iron, cobalt, silver, plati-
num and gold, have been used in this reaction. The use of
chiral metal complexes made possible enantioselective ver-
sions of the reaction.
1g More recent research described a
metal-free Doyle–Kirmse reaction using light-mediated di-
azo decomposition that generates free carbene species.1h,i A
literature survey revealed that among the different sub-
strates used in this reaction, aryl and alkyl sulfides repre-
sent the overwhelming majori ty, while derivatives bearing
an electron-withdrawing group (EWG) on the sulfur have
been sparsely reported (Scheme 1, A). This may be due to
the concern that the sulfur, depleted by an electron-with-
drawing substituent, would be less reactive toward the
electrophilic metal carbene species. However, allyl and
propargyl trifluoromethyl sulfides were successfully used
in enantioselective Doyle–Kirmse reactions employing chi-
ral rhodium or copper complexes (Scheme 1, B).
2 Another
example, that we recently reported, concerned propargyl
thiocyanates (Scheme 1, C).3 In this case, the products were
not isolated, as they subsequently rearranged to the iso-
thiocyanate derivatives via a thio-Claisen reaction. Interest-
ingly, when S-allyl or S-propargyl thioacetates were reacted
with aryl diazoketones, the S-ylide formation was followed
by sulfur-to-oxygen acyl transfer, and not by the [2,3]-rear-
rangement, thus leading to al kenyl sulfides instead of the
expected products (Scheme 1, D).4
These literature data prompted us to investigate the re-
activity of S-allyl and S-propargyl phosphorothioates, as
new electron-poor sulfide substrates, toward -diazocar-
bonyl compounds.
Moreover, the phosphorothioates, which belong to the
class of P(V) organophosphorus compounds, 5 have found
important applications  as biologically active molecules in
agrochemical and pharmaceutical fields. 6 Their prepara-
tion, as well as their uses as synthetic intermediates in vari-
ous transformations, most of  which involving the cleavage
of the P–S or C–S bond, have been independently reviewed
in 2018 by O’Sullivan and co-workers, and by our group.
7
Two other reviews that followed dealt with modern meth-
ods to access phosphorothioa tes by phosphorus–sulfur
bond formation and by direct  phosphorothiolation reac-
tions, respectively.8 A recently reported  synthesis of phos-

The reaction of a phosphorothioate with the metallo-
carbene resulting from diaz o compound decomposition
would, in the first step, lead to a phosphoryl sulfonium
ylide which, to our knowledge, is still an unknown species.
The so-formed S-ylide can then evolve along three possible
pathways: [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement yielding the
Doyle–Kirmse reaction product I, S-to-O phosphoryl trans-
fer (similar to the acyl transfer), leading to the alkenyl phos-
phate II, or S-to-C phosphoryl group migration,
10 resulting
in the -sulfanyl phosphonate III (Scheme 1, E). Herein, we
describe the rhodium-catalyzed reaction of S-allyl and S-
propargyl phosphorothioates with diazoesters, leading ex-
clusively to the Doyle–Kirmse [2,3]-rearrangement prod-
ucts I.
To set up the reaction conditions, easily available O,O-
diisopropyl S-propargyl phosphorothioate ( 1a) was select-
ed as a model substrate. Initial experiments were per-
formed by adding 2-diazo-2-phenylacetate 3a (1.5 equiv) to
a solution of 1a (1.0 equiv) in toluene ( c = 0.1 M), in the
presence of Rh
2(OAc)4 (1 mol%) as a catalyst, to ensure ef-
fective diazo decomposition to  generate rhodium carbene
(Table 1, entry 1). After only 10 minutes, 1H NMR spectro-
scopic analysis of the crude mixture revealed full conver-
sion of the diazo partner 3a and the expected homoallenyl
phosphorothioate 4aa was identified as the major product
of a complex crude reaction mixture (31%, 1H NMR yield)
and was isolated in 31% yield. With this result in hand, opti-
mization studies were conducte d further. First, the nature
of the ligand on the rhodium dimer catalyst was investigat-
ed, switching from acetate (OAc) to the bulky pivalate
(OPiv) or to the electro-deficient trifluoroacetate (TFA). The
use of the first complex led to a higher conversion com-
pared to the acetate, however a lower 1H NMR yield was
measured (entry 2 vs 1), while the second complex led to a
lower conversion and yield (entry 3 vs 1). We selected the
Rh2(OAc)4 for further experiments, as it represented the
best compromise between conv ersion and yield. Then, the
influence of the number of eq uivalents of di azoester part-
ner 3a was investigated in an attempt to increase the con-
version of 1a to completion. Indeed, increasing from 1.5 to
2.0 equivalents of 3a substantially improved conversion and
yield (entry 1 vs 4 and 5). With 4.0 equivalents full conver-
sion (>99%) of the starting phosphorothioate 1a was
reached and 4aa was obtained in 70% yield (entry 6). To fur-
ther improve the yield of the transformation, the impact of
the solvent was investigated. To our surprise, a switch from
toluene to dichloromethane was detrimental to the reac-
tion as only 12% of 4aa was actually obtained and a fast de-
composition and dimerization of the diazo partner was ob-
served (entry 7). Dichloroethane (DCE) was then tested and
resulted in a smooth diazo decomposition with full conver-
sion (>99%) of the starting material 1a, leading to 4aa in a
good isolated yield of 85% (ent ry 8). It is worth noting that
the use of DCE also reduced the reaction time from 10 min-
utes to 5 minutes. When lowering the catalytic charge to
only 0.1 mol%, the reaction was still efficient, with a con-
version of 98% and an NMR yield of 80% (entry 9). The na-
ture of the metal catalyst was also investigated by testing
the ruthenium(II) complex [( η
6-C6H6)RuCl(-Cl)]2, copper
thiophene-2-carboxylate, silver triflate and palladium(II)
chloride, but in all cases no conversion of the starting mate-
rial 1a was observed (Table 1, en tries 10–13). In the case of
the Ru, Ag and Pd catalysts, diazoester decomposition oc-
curred and led to dimerization of the carbene, while with
CuTC the diazoester was recovere d. Finally, we kept the re-
action conditions given in en try 8 for our further experi-
ments.
With these optimal conditions in hand, several struc-
tural modifications of the reac tion partners were investi-
gated to explore the scope and limitations of the transfor-
mation (Scheme 2). Changing the isopropyl groups on the
phosphoryl of 1 to ethyl or 
L-menthyl groups did not
change the reactivity, leading to similar yields. Unfortunate-
ly, the asymmetric Doyle–Kirmse reaction using dimenthyl
phosphorothioate 1c as the chiral substrate was not diaste-

We then examined the efficiency of the reaction in the
S-allyl series, by using different phosphorothioates 2a–f
and the diazoester partner 3a. Starting from substrate 2a,
the S-homoallyl derivative 5aa was obtained in a good yield
of 83%. When S-crotyl 2b (77:23 ratio of E/Z-isomers) and
S-cinnamyl phosphorothioates 2c (100% E-isomer) were
used, slightly lower yields were reached, 65% for 5ba and
50% for 5ca. In both cases, no diastereoselectivity was ob-
served, and products 5ba and 5ca were obtained as mix-
tures of diastereomers in ~1:1  ratio. On the other hand, S-
dimethylhomoallyl phosphorothioate 5da was obtained in
a good yield of 82% from the S-prenyl precursor 2d, without
any detection of deprenylated byproducts in the crude reac-
tion mixture, as previously reported for the phenyl sulfide
series.
12 The S-methallyl 2e and S-bromoallyl 2f substrates
also led to the corresponding S-homoallyl phosphorothio-
ates, in 44% and 67% yield, respectively.
To showcase the robustness and practicality of our meth-
od, the reaction was scaled up to 1 mmol of sulfide 1a and 4
mmol of diazoester 3a, using only 0.1 mol% of Rh catalyst. In
this case, 20 minutes was necessary for a complete conver-
sion and phosphorothioate 4aa was isolated in 64% yield.
Taking advantage of the presence of the carboxylate and
the double bond functionalitie s in the obtained products,
we engaged an S-homoallyl phosphorothioate in an intra-
molecular Brønsted acid catalyzed hydroacyloxylation to
access a lactone. By treating phosphorothioate 5ea with 1
equivalent of p-toluenesulfonic acid  (PTSA) monohydrate,
5-exo-trig cyclization was achieved efficiently, leading to
the expected lactone 6ea in 62% yield (Scheme 3).

In summary, we have developed a rhodium-catalyzed
Doyle–Kirmse reaction of S-allyl and S-propargyl phospho-
rothioates with aryl diazoace tates. This represents a rare
example of Doyle–Kirmse reaction involving derivatives
bearing an electron-withdrawing group on sulfur. The
transformation occurs under mild conditions, at room tem-
perature, in only 5 minutes, and exhibits a good substrate
tolerance. It led via the [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of
sulfonium ylides to various S-homoallyl and S-homoallenyl
phosphorothioates (19 examples) in yields ranging from
25% to 92%. To illustrate the potential post-functionaliza-
tion of the obtained products, a phosphorothioate-substi-
tuted lactone was prepared by acid-catalyzed cyclization of
the carboxylate function onto the homoallyl double bond.
From an organic synthesis point of view, this reaction is a
practical method toward accessing a series of compounds
containing a quaternary carb on stereocenter bearing a
phosphorothioate functional group, which is of interest in
drug design, and as a route to introduce P and/or S into mol-
ecules.

Abstract The Doyle–Kirmse reaction represents a powerful synthetic
tool for forming both C–S and C–C bonds in a single process. The rhodi-
um-catalyzed Doyle–Kirmse reaction of S-allyl and S-propargyl phos-
phorothioates with diazoesters has been developed and represents a
rare example involving substrates bearing an electron-withdrawing
group on the sulfur atom. The transformation takes place at room tem-
perature, in only 5 minutes, and leads via a [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrange-
ment of the sulfonium ylide intermediate to the corresponding S-ho-
moallyl or S-homoallenyl phosphorothioates in yields ranging from 25%
to 92% (19 examples).

Key words Doyle–Kirmse reaction, [2,3]-rearrangement, propargyl
sulfides, allyl sulfides, diazoesters, phosphorothioates, C–S bond forma-
tion

The Doyle–Kirmse reaction is a powerful method for
forming both C–S and C–C bonds in a single process, en-
abling the synthesis of a wide range of homoallyl or ho-
moallenyl sulfides.<sup>1</sup> The metal-catalyzed version consists of
the reaction of an allyl or a propargyl sulfide and a metal
carbene species classically generated by the decomposition
of a diazo compound (Scheme 1, A). This leads to the key in-
termediate of this reaction which is a sulfonium ylide that
can be either metal-bound or metal-free depending mainly
on the nature of the substrate and metal. The resulting ylide
can then evolve through a [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement
to the corresponding homoallyl or homoallenyl sulfide. Var-
ious transition-metal complexes, mainly based on rhodium
and copper, but also on ruthenium, iron, cobalt, silver, plati-
num and gold, have been used in this reaction. The use of
chiral metal complexes made possible enantioselective ver-
sions of the reaction.<sup>1g</sup> More recent research described a
metal-free Doyle–Kirmse reaction using light-mediated di-
azo decomposition that generates free carbene species.<sup>1h,i</sup> A

literature survey revealed that among the different sub-
strates used in this reaction, aryl and alkyl sulfides repre-
sent the overwhelming majority, while derivatives bearing
an electron-withdrawing group (EWG) on the sulfur have
been sparsely reported (Scheme 1, A). This may be due to
the concern that the sulfur, depleted by an electron-with-
drawing substituent, would be less reactive toward the
electrophilic metal carbene species. However, allyl and
propargyl trifluoromethyl sulfides were successfully used
in enantioselective Doyle–Kirmse reactions employing chi-
ral rhodium or copper complexes (Scheme 1, B).<sup>2</sup> Another
example, that we recently reported, concerned propargyl
thiocyanates (Scheme 1, C).<sup>3</sup> In this case, the products were
not isolated, as they subsequently rearranged to the iso-
thiocyanate derivatives via a thio-Claisen reaction. Interest-
ingly, when S-allyl or S-propargyl thioacetates were reacted
with aryl diazoketones, the S-ylide formation was followed
by sulfur-to-oxygen acyl transfer, and not by the [2,3]-rear-
rangement, thus leading to alkenyl sulfides instead of the
expected products (Scheme 1, D).<sup>4</sup>

These literature data prompted us to investigate the re-
activity of S-allyl and S-propargyl phosphorothioates, as
new electron-poor sulfide substrates, toward -diazocar-
bonyl compounds.

Moreover, the phosphorothioates, which belong to the
class of P(V) organophosphorus compounds,<sup>5</sup> have found
important applications as biologically active molecules in
agrochemical and pharmaceutical fields.<sup>6</sup> Their prepara-
tion, as well as their uses as synthetic intermediates in vari-
ous transformations, most of which involving the cleavage
of the P–S or C–S bond, have been independently reviewed
in 2018 by O’Sullivan and co-workers, and by our group.<sup>7</sup>
Two other reviews that followed dealt with modern meth-
ods to access phosphorothioates by phosphorus–sulfur
bond formation and by direct phosphorothiolation reac-
tions, respectively.<sup>8</sup> A recently reported synthesis of phos-

In summary, we have developed a rhodium-catalyzed
Doyle–Kirmse reaction of S-allyl and S-propargyl phospho-
rothioates with aryl diazoacetates. This represents a rare
example of Doyle–Kirmse reaction involving derivatives
bearing an electron-withdrawing group on sulfur. The
transformation occurs under mild conditions, at room tem-
perature, in only 5 minutes, and exhibits a good substrate
tolerance. It led via the [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of
sulfonium ylides to various S-homoallyl and S-homoallenyl
phosphorothioates (19 examples) in yields ranging from
25% to 92%. To illustrate the potential post-functionaliza-
tion of the obtained products, a phosphorothioate-substi-
tuted lactone was prepared by acid-catalyzed cyclization of
the carboxylate function onto the homoallyl double bond.

From an organic synthesis point of view, this reaction is a
practical method toward accessing a series of compounds
containing a quaternary carbon stereocenter bearing a
phosphorothioate functional group, which is of interest in
drug design, and as a route to introduce P and/or S into mol-
ecules.
